div.head: Oliver Herford
div.p: Fig. 28

lg.l: 'S
Albert Edward, well meaning but flighty,

div.p: Who invited King Arthur, the blameless and mighty,
To meet Alcibiades and Aphrodite.
Fig. 28

lg.l: is for Bernhardt, who fails to awaken

div.p: Much feeling in Bismarck, Barabbas, and Bacon.
Fig. 28

lg.l: is Columbus, who tries to explain

div.p: How to balance an egg—to the utter disdain
Of Confucius, Carlyle, Cleopatra, and Cain.
Fig. 28

lg.l: 'S
for Diogenes, Darwin, and Dante,

div.p: Who delight in the dance Of a Darling Bacchante.

lg.l: is for Edison, making believe

div.p: He's invented a clever contrivance for Eve,
Who complained that she never could laugh in her sleeve.

lg.l: is for Franklin, who fearfully shocks

div.p: The feelings of Fenelon, Faber, and Fox.

lg.l: is Godiva, whose great bareback feat

div.p: Though Gounod and Goldsmith implore and entreat.

lg.l: is for Handel, who pours out his soul

div.p: Through the bagpipes to Howells and Homer, who roll
On the floor in an ecstasy past all control.

lg.l: is for Ibsen, reciting a play

div.p: While Irving and Ingersoll hasten away.

lg.l: is for Johnson, who only says "Pish!"

div.p: To Jonah, who tells him his tale of a fish.

lg.l: is the Kaiser, who kindly repeats

div.p: Some original verses to Kipling and Keats.

lg.l: is Lafontaine, who finds he's unable

div.p: To interest Luther and Liszt in his fable,
While Loie continues to dance on the table.

lg.l: is Macduff, who's prevailed upon Milton

div.p: And Montaigne and Manon to each try a kilt on.

lg.l: is Napoleon, shrouded in gloom,

div.p: With Nero, Narcissus, and Nordau, to whom
He's explaining the manual of arms with a broom.

lg.l: is for Oliver, casting aspersion

div.p: On Omar, that awfully dissolute Persian,
Though secretly longing to join the diversion.

lg.l: is for Peter, who hollers "No! No!"

div.p: Through the keyhole to Paine, Paderewski, and Poe.

lg.l: is the Queen, so noble and free—

div.p: For further particulars look under V.

lg.l: 'S
Rubenstein, playing that old thing in F

div.p: To Rollo and Rembrandt, who wish they were deaf.

lg.l: 'S
is for Swinburne, who, seeking the true,
the good, and the beautiful, visits the Zoo,

div.p: Where he chances on Sappho and Mr. Sardou,
And Socrates, all with the same end in view.

lg.l: is for Talleyrand toasting Miss Truth,

div.p: By the side of her well, in a glass of vermouth,
And presenting Mark Twain as the friend of his youth.

lg.l: is for Undine, pursuing Ulysses

div.p: And Umberto, who flee her damp, death-dealing kisses.

lg.l: is Victoria, noble and true—

div.p: For further particulars look under Q.

lg.l: 'S
Wagner, who sang and played lots for
Washington, Wesley, and good Doctor Watts.

div.p: His prurient plots pained Wesley and Watts,
But Washington said he "enjoyed them in spots."

lg.l: is Xantippe, who's having her say,

div.p: His prurient plots pained Wesley and Watts,
And frightening the army of Xerxes away.

lg.l: is for Young, the great Mormon saint,

div.p: Who thinks little Yum Yum and Yvette so quaint,
He has to be instantly held in restraint.

lg.l: is for Zola, presenting La Terre

div.p: To Zenobia the brave and Zuleika the fair,
Whose blushes they artfully conceal with their hair.
